problem.title: XDP In-Kernel SYN Flood & DDoS Packet Dropping
problem.prompt: Your Linux edge load balancers (16 vCPU, 25 Gbps NICs) are hit by a spoofed 20,000,000 PPS TCP SYN flood. Your existing `iptables` + `nf_conntrack` rules saturate 100% SoftIRQ CPU (`ksoftirqd`) within seconds, exhaust the 262K-entry `nf_conntrack` table, and drop 95% of legitimate customer HTTPS connections—even though bandwidth is under 12 Gbps. Design an XDP/eBPF in-kernel mitigation pipeline that drops the 20M PPS flood while keeping legitimate traffic healthy under <15% CPU.

spark.summary: Move SYN flood filtering out of iptables/nf_conntrack into a Native XDP eBPF program using a Per-CPU LPM CIDR blocklist, stateless SYN-flood rate limits, and ringbuf drop sampling.
spark.keyTakeaway: When traffic spikes expose hidden coupling, drop spoofed SYN floods via XDP_DROP before sk_buff or nf_conntrack allocation, and use Per-CPU maps + atomic link pinning for zero-downtime rule updates.
spark.byteSummary:
A 20M PPS small-packet SYN flood exhausts CPU and kernel tables long before it saturates 25 Gbps link bandwidth. Because `iptables` runs *after* `sk_buff` allocation and `nf_conntrack` insertion, each spoofed SYN allocates kernel memory and contends on conntrack hash-bucket locks, pegging `ksoftirqd` at 100% CPU and starving legitimate HTTPS handshakes.

Moving mitigation to **Native XDP** inside the NIC driver intercepts packets before `sk_buff` or `nf_conntrack` exists. A lightweight XDP program parses Ethernet/IPv4/TCP headers with Verifier-safe bounds checks, matches known-bad CIDRs in `BPF_MAP_TYPE_LPM_TRIE`, and tracks per-CPU SYN rates using `BPF_MAP_TYPE_PERCPU_HASH` (or issues stateless **XDP SYN-cookies** via `XDP_TX` for suspicious bursts).

Flood packets return `XDP_DROP` (~20M PPS across 16 cores at <15% CPU), while legitimate established flows and clean SYNs return `XDP_PASS` into the kernel stack (optionally with `NOTRACK` / `tcp_syncookies=1` backup). A user-space Go/Python control plane updates the LPM blocklist atomically and reads 1-in-10,000 drop samples from `BPF_MAP_TYPE_RINGBUF`.

The core trade-off is collateral false-positive risk vs survival: stateless XDP rate limits or coarse `/24` LPM blocks can affect NAT-shared users if thresholds are too tight, so always pair XDP with an explicit allowlist map, sampled drop telemetry, and a dead-man rollback timer.

explanation.foundation: 20M 64-byte SYN packets use only `~10.2 Gbps` of wire bandwidth, yet crash a 25 Gbps Linux host because:

learningJourney.title: Pre-sk_buff XDP Pipeline: Allowlist -> LPM Blocklist -> SYN Rate Check
learningJourney.purpose: Order XDP packet checks from cheapest/safest to stateful so clean traffic flows with minimal latency.

explanation.foundation: Structure the Native XDP filter in three deterministic fast-path stages:
explanation.core:
1. **Trusted Allowlist (`BPF_MAP_TYPE_LPM_TRIE`)**: Health checks, internal VPCs, and CDN edges immediately return `XDP_PASS`.
2. **Dynamic CIDR Blocklist (`BPF_MAP_TYPE_LPM_TRIE`)**: Known botnet prefixes return `XDP_DROP` in <30 ns.
3. **TCP SYN-Only Filter**: Non-SYN packets (established `ACK`/`PSH` flows) bypass rate checks immediately (`XDP_PASS`). Only pure `TCP_SYN` packets (`syn && !ack`) enter per-CPU token-bucket/rate accounting.

decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Use a single unpartitioned path with unbounded retries and synchronous global coordination.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Global coordination serializes throughput under load, while unbounded retries amplify transient stalls into full outages.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Compare synchronous strict-consistency paths against bounded asynchronous replication, local caching, or partitioned ownership.

learningJourney.title: Handling Spoofed Source IPs with XDP SYN-Cookies (`XDP_TX`)
learningJourney.purpose: Defend against randomized spoofed source IPs that evade per-IP rate limiters.

explanation.foundation: When an attacker randomizes source IPs across all `2^32` addresses, per-IP rate limits never trigger on any single IP. Under global SYN-rate threshold breach (`global_syn_pps > 500K`):
explanation.core:
- **XDP SYN-Proxy / Cookie**: XDP computes a cryptographic **SYN-cookie** (`SipHash(src_ip, src_port, dst_ip, dst_port, secret, minute)`) as the TCP Initial Sequence Number, swaps MAC/IP/Port headers, and bounces a `SYN-ACK` back out the NIC via **`XDP_TX`**—without allocating any kernel socket.
- Spoofed bots never reply with the final `ACK`; real clients send `ACK` with `ack_seq == cookie + 1`, which XDP verifies before handing the handshake to the kernel.

learningJourney.title: Per-CPU Drop Counters & Sampled Ringbuf Telemetry
learningJourney.purpose: Observe dropped attack traffic without saturating CPU or missing packets in tcpdump.

explanation.foundation: Since `tcpdump` cannot see `XDP_DROP` frames, emit lightweight visibility without slowing the 20M PPS hot path:
explanation.core:
- **Per-CPU Counters**: Increment `PERCPU_ARRAY[DROP_SYN_FLOOD]` in L1 cache (0 locks).
- **1-in-10,000 Ringbuf Sampling**: Only when `(counter & 0x3FFF) == 0`, copy the 54-byte header into `BPF_MAP_TYPE_RINGBUF` for user-space inspection and automated `/24` botnet CIDR extraction.

learningJourney.title: Multi-Queue NIC RSS Hashing & NUMA IRQ Pinning
learningJourney.purpose: Distribute 20M PPS evenly across all 16 cores via NIC Receive Side Scaling (RSS).

explanation.foundation: If all NIC RX packets land on Queue 0 (Core 0), even XDP caps out at ~1.5–3M PPS on that single core:
explanation.core:
- **Enable 16 RX Queues (`ethtool -L eth0 combined 16`)**: Hardware RSS hashes the 5-tuple across 16 queues, pinning 1 queue per CPU core.
- **Disable `irqbalance` Drift**: Pin each RX queue's IRQ affinity directly to its NUMA-local core so XDP runs lock-free on `PERCPU` maps at 20M+ PPS total.

problem.title: XDP In-Kernel SYN Flood & DDoS Packet Dropping
problem.prompt: Your Linux edge load balancers (16 vCPU, 25 Gbps NICs) are hit by a spoofed 20,000,000 PPS TCP SYN flood. Your existing `iptables` + `nf_conntrack` rules saturate 100% SoftIRQ CPU (`ksoftirqd`) within seconds, exhaust the 262K-entry `nf_conntrack` table, and drop 95% of legitimate customer HTTPS connections—even though bandwidth is under 12 Gbps. Design an XDP/eBPF in-kernel mitigation pipeline that drops the 20M PPS flood while keeping legitimate traffic healthy under <15% CPU.
